subject: Biology
title: Basic Ecology
outline: Define ecology and its basic terms: habitat, niche, population, community, ecosystem, biosphere
Describe the major biomes of the world and the Nigerian vegetation belts
Distinguish biotic and abiotic factors and their measuring instruments
Construct food chains, food webs, trophic levels and ecological pyramids
Explain energy flow and the 10 % law
Describe simple field methods for estimating population size

modules.title: Ecological Concepts and Biomes
modules.html:
1. Basic Terms

  • Ecology – the study of the relationship between organisms and their environment.
  • Habitat – the natural home of an organism (pond, forest floor, tree bark).
  • Ecological niche – the functional role and position of an organism in its habitat, including what it eats, when it is active and how it interacts with others.
  • Population – all individuals of one species in a given area at a given time.
  • Community – all populations living and interacting in an area.
  • Ecosystem – a community plus its non-living environment functioning as a unit.
  • Biosphere – the part of the earth (lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere) that supports life.

2. Components of an Ecosystem

  1. Producers (autotrophs) – green plants and algae.
  2. Consumers – primary (herbivores), secondary and tertiary (carnivores), omnivores.
  3. Decomposers – bacteria and fungi returning nutrients to the soil.
  4. Abiotic components – light, temperature, water, air, soil, pH, salinity.

3. Major Biomes

BiomeClimateTypical organisms
Tropical rainforestHeavy rainfall (>2000 mm), high temperatureTall buttressed trees, lianas, epiphytes, monkeys
Savanna (grassland)Seasonal rain, distinct dry seasonGrasses, scattered fire-resistant trees, grazers
DesertRainfall <250 mm, extreme temperature rangeCacti, succulents, camel, rodents
Temperate forest / grasslandModerate, four seasonsDeciduous trees, bison, deer
Tundra / ArcticVery cold, permafrostLichens, mosses, reindeer
Aquatic (marine, estuarine, freshwater)Water-basedPlankton, fish, mangroves

From south to north Nigeria shows: mangrove/swamp forest → rainforest → derived savanna → Guinea savanna → Sudan savanna → Sahel savanna, reflecting a decreasing rainfall gradient.

examples.q: Differentiate between habitat and ecological niche using the earthworm.
examples.a: The habitat of the earthworm is moist humus-rich topsoil — the physical place where it lives. Its niche is its role there: it feeds on decaying organic matter, burrows and aerates the soil at night, is prey to birds, and recycles nutrients through its castings.

examples.q: Why does the vegetation of Nigeria change from south to north?
examples.a: Rainfall amount and duration decrease steadily northwards while temperature range and evaporation increase. Plants adapted to abundant water (tall broad-leaved trees) dominate the south, while drought-resistant grasses and thorny trees dominate the north.

modules.title: Biotic and Abiotic Factors and Their Measurement
modules.html:
1. Abiotic Factors

FactorInstrumentEffect
TemperatureThermometerControls enzyme activity, distribution
Light intensityPhotometer/light meterControls photosynthesis, flowering
Relative humidityHygrometerAffects transpiration and water loss
Wind speed/directionAnemometer, wind vanePollination, dispersal, evaporation
RainfallRain gaugeWater availability
pHpH meter, universal indicatorNutrient availability, species distribution
Water currentFlow meter/floatAquatic distribution and adaptation
SalinityHydrometer/conductivity meterDetermines marine, estuarine, freshwater species
Depth/turbidityMetre rule, Secchi discLight penetration in water

2. Biotic Factors and Interactions

  • Competition – intraspecific (same species) or interspecific (different species) for light, food, water, mates, space.
  • Predation – one organism kills and eats another; regulates prey numbers.
  • Parasitism – (+/−) parasite benefits, host harmed.
  • Mutualism – (+/+) both benefit, e.g. lichens, rumen bacteria.
  • Commensalism – (+/0) one benefits, the other unaffected, e.g. epiphytic orchid on a tree.
  • Saprophytism and symbiosis in decomposition and nutrient cycling.

3. Field Methods

  • Quadrat – a square frame used to estimate density, frequency and percentage cover of sessile organisms. Estimated population = mean number per quadrat × (total area / quadrat area).
  • Line and belt transects – record changes in vegetation along an environmental gradient.
  • Capture–mark–recapture (Lincoln index) for mobile animals:
$$N = \frac{n_1 \times n_2}{m}$$

where \(n_1\) is the number first marked, \(n_2\) the number captured on the second occasion and \(m\) the marked individuals recaptured.

examples.q: 120 grasshoppers were caught, marked and released. Later 90 were caught, of which 30 were marked. Estimate the population.
examples.a: \( N = \dfrac{n_1 n_2}{m} = \dfrac{120 \times 90}{30} = 360 \) grasshoppers. Assumptions: marks do not wear off or harm the animal, marked individuals mix randomly, and there is no significant migration, birth or death between samplings.

examples.q: A 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrat thrown 10 times gave a mean of 8 seedlings. Estimate the number in 200 m².
examples.a: Area of quadrat = 0.25 m², so density = 8/0.25 = 32 seedlings m⁻². In 200 m² the estimated population is \( 32 \times 200 = 6400 \) seedlings.

modules.title: Food Chains, Webs and Energy Flow
modules.html:
1. Trophic Levels

A food chain shows the linear transfer of energy: producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer → decomposer. Example: grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk. Arrows point in the direction of energy flow. A food web is a network of interconnected food chains and is more realistic because most organisms eat, and are eaten by, several species.

2. Energy Flow and the 10 % Law

Energy enters an ecosystem as sunlight; only 1–2 % of incident light is fixed by producers. At each transfer roughly 90 % of the energy is lost as heat, in respiration, movement, excretion and to uneaten parts, so only about 10 % passes on:

$$\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\text{energy in next trophic level}}{\text{energy in previous trophic level}} \times 100\%$$

Consequently food chains rarely exceed four or five links, and energy flow is unidirectional while nutrients are cycled.

3. Ecological Pyramids

  • Pyramid of numbers – counts organisms at each level; may be inverted (one tree supporting many insects).
  • Pyramid of biomass – dry mass per level; usually upright on land, may be inverted in the sea where phytoplankton reproduce quickly.
  • Pyramid of energy – always upright, because energy is lost at every transfer.

4. Biological Importance

Decomposers release nutrients locked in dead tissue back to the soil, sustaining producers. Removal of a species from a web (for example a predator) can cause the prey population to explode and vegetation to be over-grazed, showing the interdependence of organisms. Persistent toxins such as DDT become concentrated up the chain (biomagnification), harming top carnivores most.

examples.q: In the chain maize → rat → snake → hawk, producers fix 20 000 kJ. Estimate the energy available to the hawk.
examples.a: Applying the 10 % law: rat \(= 20\,000 \times 0.1 = 2000\,\text{kJ}\); snake \(= 200\,\text{kJ}\); hawk \(= 20\,\text{kJ}\). This steep loss explains why top carnivores are few in number.

examples.q: Why is the pyramid of energy never inverted?
examples.a: Energy obeys the laws of thermodynamics: some is always lost as heat at each transfer, so a trophic level can never contain more energy than the one below it. Numbers and biomass can be inverted because size and turnover rate differ between levels.

quiz.q: The functional role of an organism in its habitat is its
quiz.solution: The niche describes how the organism lives and interacts, not merely where it lives.

quiz.q: All the living organisms interacting in a given area constitute a
quiz.solution: A community is made up of all the populations in an area.

quiz.q: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
quiz.solution: pH is a non-living chemical factor of the environment.

quiz.q: The instrument used to measure relative humidity is the
quiz.solution: A hygrometer (wet-and-dry bulb) measures atmospheric humidity.

quiz.q: Wind speed is measured with a
quiz.solution: An anemometer measures speed; a wind vane shows direction.

quiz.q: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk, the lizard is a
quiz.solution: It feeds on the herbivorous grasshopper, making it a second-order consumer.

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?
quiz.solution: About 90 % is lost as heat and in metabolism, so roughly 10 % is passed on.
Energy always decreases with each transfer, so its pyramid cannot be inverted.

quiz.q: Bacteria and fungi that break down dead organisms are called
quiz.solution: They release nutrients from dead matter back into the ecosystem.

quiz.q: The relationship between a lichen's alga and fungus is
quiz.solution: The alga supplies food by photosynthesis while the fungus provides anchorage, water and mineral salts.

quiz.q: An orchid growing on the branch of a tree without harming it illustrates
quiz.solution: The epiphyte gains support and light; the tree is unaffected.

quiz.q: A quadrat is best used to sample
quiz.solution: Quadrats work for organisms that do not move away, such as herbs and grasses.

quiz.q: Using the Lincoln index, if 50 fish were marked, 40 later caught and 10 were marked, the population is
The vegetation belt with the lowest annual rainfall in Nigeria is the
quiz.solution: The Sahel in the extreme north receives the least rain and has scattered thorny shrubs.

quiz.q: Energy flow through an ecosystem is described as
quiz.solution: Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat; it is not recycled like nutrients.

quiz.q: The accumulation of DDT to harmful levels in top carnivores is called
quiz.solution: Persistent, fat-soluble toxins become more concentrated at each successive trophic level.
